newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Kikkoman sees profit recovery from 1998.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Kikkoman sees profit recovery from 1998.

text.p: Kikkoman Corp, the world's top-selling soy sauce maker, expects profits to start picking up in 1998 after a tough few years as investment in new plants and products seeps through to the bottom line.

Kikkoman president Yuzaburo Mogi told Reuters in an interview that although group operating profits may be flat in the current business year to the end of December, the company's next set of annual results should show a modest recovery.
"Last year and this year should be the bottom," Mogi said. "I hope (group operating) profits will increase maybe by 10 percent (in 1998)," he said in an interview on Monday evening.
Kikkoman's business year runs from January to December.
The shorter-term profit picture is clouded by a rise in the cost of soybeans as well as an increase in Japan's sales tax in April to five percent from three percent, he said.

In the year to end-December 1996, Kikkoman made a group net profit of 7.29 billion yen, compared with 4.45 billion yen a year earlier. On an operating level, however, group profits fell to 9.61 billion yen in 1996 from 10.79 billion yen.
The company's latest forecast for 1997 is for a group net profit of 6.60 billion yen, but it has not given an official estimate for group operating profits.

Asked whether the company was on track for its forecast, Mogi said: "Yes, (but) maybe a little bit behind target, but of course better than last year." He did not give specific figures, saying it was still early to assess the outlook.

Heavy investment in building a second plant in the United States and a new factory in the Netherlands to serve the European market have acted as a drag on earnings, but the benefit should flow through in a year or two, he said.

Tapping overseas markets and developing a steady stream of new soy-based products, such as marinades and dipping sauces for meat, are the key to future prosperity as the home market for basic soy sauce is saturated, he said.

The company is targeting markets in Europe, particularly Scandinavia, and is confident there is room to keep boosting sales in the United States, where Kikkoman has had production facilities since the 1970s, he said.

"This year and next, profit from international business might decrease, but not much," he said, citing the investment in expanding overseas production and the higher cost of soybeans. "But then maybe from 1999 profits from the international business will start growing again."

Kikkoman is Japan's biggest soy sauce maker, with a market share of just under 30 percent, but has been struggling to stem a drop in domestic sales due to stiff competition from cheaper brands and a shrinking home market for its staple product.

Poor sales of Del Monte brand products, for which Kikkoman owns marketing rights in Asia, have also proved a stubborn problem. Mogi conceded that Del Monte sales had been disappointing but said Kikkoman was working on new products in that range to turn things around.

"Price competition (in Japan) for existing products is very tough," Mogi said. "We have to develop new products which should be high value-added and we would like to sell those products not by price competition but through advertising."
Although upbeat about the firm's international prospects, analysts agreed Kikkoman would probably turn in a lacklustre earnings performance in 1997.

"I think we're looking at pretty much flat development of Kikkoman's numbers," said Patricia Horvath, an analyst at UBS Global Research. "The best of the international will be held back by the worst of the domestic."

Analysts also had some qualms about its new product strategy, saying for example that the company could encounter stiff competition from established makers in Japan with its new sauces for Korean-style "yakiniku" barbecue beef.
"It looks a bit dangerous," said Keiko Sasaki, an analyst at ING Barings, citing possibly thin profit margins.
"The minute they come out with a new product they will have a competitor right behind them," said Horvath of UBS. "They will have to be very swift on their feet."
